states.name: empty
states.gap: Title carries zero file-type signal — a bare 110px 'Untitled' means a .md and a .txt of the same name render as the identical 8 glyphs in the bar, where A's 48px of '.md' at least disambiguates them at a glance. B's canvas is also 2 levels darker (#F7F7F7 vs #F9F9F9), which drops the #8C8C8C chrome ink to a marginally lower contrast ratio against it.
states.gapTheirs: Title bar prints the filesystem extension: 'Untitled.md' measures 157px where B's 'Untitled' is 110px — 48px of '.md' (x=1459–1506) parked in the one centred slot the bar exists for. Worse, the string is centred as a whole, so the document's actual name spans x=1351–1455 with its optical centre at ~1403, sitting ~37px left of the window's 1440px axis; the name a writer looks for is never on the axis, and drifts further with every longer filename.
states.verdict: This is the same chrome twice — same 26×24 toggle at x=34, same 52×24 View control at x=2794, same #8C8C8C, same 17px stats band with the number at #4A4A4A over the label at #8C8C8C — so the whole judgement collapses onto eleven glyphs versus eight. A's title bar is doing the file manager's job instead of the writer's: '.md' is a fact about storage, not about the piece, and centring the full string leaves the name itself 37px off-axis, which is exactly the kind of drift a typographer sees before they see the word. Neither side draws a hairline anywhere — a single-pixel column at x=2400 runs one flat grey from y=0 to y=1799 in both — so neither bar is actually separated from the page it sits against, and neither pretends to be. B wins on the one thing that differs, and it's a thin win.

states.name: typing
states.gap: The page runs right into the chrome: A's last body line stops 9 device px (4.5 logical) above the stats hairline, against B's 33 device px (16.5 logical) — the rule reads as a lid clamped on the line rather than a bar the page passes under. states.gapTheirs: No weight step between figure and label. For the identical string '188' at identical 17 px cap height, A's digits carry 323 dark pixels / 16,639 ink units against B's 266 / 13,119 — A's numbers are ~21% fatter in stroke, reading semibold against a light label; B's digits are barely heavier than 'words'. The greys are not the differentiator (number #B5B5B5 vs #B6B6B6, label #CECECE vs #CFCFCF, within one level), so B's count is carried on colour alone and the number stops leading its cell.
states.verdict: These two bars are near-clones — same 26 px height, same half-pixel hairline at the same 9-level contrast, same 4 px number-to-label and ~16 px cell-to-cell gutters, both locked to the 1440 px centre axis, both correctly dropping the title bar and leaving the bar ends empty. The one thing that separates them is the thing the bar exists for: A's figures are set heavy enough that the number arrives before the label at a glance, while B's '188' and 'words' read as one grey run you have to parse. Against that, A lets the rule crowd the last line to within 4.5 px, which a writer feels the moment the cursor reaches the bottom of the window. Weak hierarchy in the only row of chrome you kept is a worse failure than a tight bottom gutter, so A — but by a hair, and A owes B a bottom margin.

B pays for its clean column with a grey scrollbar nailed to the edge of the paper, which is chrome a writer did not ask for, but it lives 600 px right of the text and does not move.

states.gapTheirs: B's menu is not anchored to the bar it came from: panel spans x2046–2418, centre 2232, while the stats cells span x1236–1643, centre 1439 — 396 logical px (793 device px) adrift, its left edge 403 device px clear of the last stats glyph, and its bottom floats 9 device px above the hairline instead of meeting the bar. states.verdict: Click the word count dead centre at the bottom of B and the menu opens four hundred points away over the right edge of your paragraph, with the bar you just clicked showing no sign it was clicked — you spend a beat working out what you hit. A ties the two together properly: pressed pill under the cells, menu centred on them to the pixel, bottom edge touching the rule. A then squanders some of that by ticking "Hide Statistics", which tells you the numbers are off while they are visibly on, and by leaving a #A6A9AA scrollbar thumb standing on the page the whole time. Still A: a stray glyph is a bug you read past, a menu that opens in the wrong place is one you stop writing for.
